bigPicture: The Nvidia crisis spread to Asia: Taiwan's stock market fell 6% and South Korea's 3.6% as investors dumped the chipmakers that supply Nvidia, while Europe held near record highs. In the Gulf the US now has three aircraft carriers in the region after Iran attacked a base in Bahrain and claimed tankers struck mines near Hormuz, yet oil stayed around $96 because the IEA expects a supply surplus. Ukraine launched one of its largest drone attacks of the year on Moscow, and in Yemen the Houthis advanced to about 70 km from Aden. Fresh data showed China's consumers and investment weakening and Japan's economy shrinking slightly, as markets brace for a likely US rate rise in December. Socially, Spain declared a migration emergency in the Canary Islands after a record day of arrivals, four Western governments pressed Israel to let 150,000 tents into flooded Gaza, and Congo's Ebola outbreak kept growing.

glossary.def: A long-term loan to buy property, secured on that property so the lender can sell it if the borrower stops paying.
glossary.example: A 400,000 zł, 25-year mortgage at 5.95% costs about 2,565 zł a month.

glossary.def: The size of a loan divided by the value of the property securing it.
glossary.example: A 480,000 zł loan on a 600,000 zł flat has an LTV of 80%.

glossary.def: The share of a borrower's net income that goes on loan payments each month.
glossary.example: Payments of 4,000 zł on income of 8,000 zł give a DSTI of 50%.

glossary.def: A loan repaid in equal regular payments, each covering that period's interest plus some principal.
glossary.example: Most Polish mortgages are annuities: early payments are mostly interest.

glossary.def: The Polish Short Term Rate, an index based on actual overnight deposit transactions, replacing WIBOR in new Polish loans.
glossary.example: Seven large Polish banks had switched new mortgages to POLSTR by 7 October 2026.

glossary.def: Rules that protect the financial system as a whole, such as limits on loan-to-value or stress tests of borrowers.
glossary.example: Poland's Recommendation S caps most mortgages at 80% LTV.

glossary.def: When a property is worth less than the loan secured on it.
glossary.example: If a flat bought with a 480,000 zł loan falls in value to 450,000 zł, the owner has negative equity.

glossary.def: A company that manufactures chips designed by other firms.

glossary.def: Spending on long-lasting physical assets such as factories, machinery, roads and buildings.

glossary.def: A growth rate for a short period expressed as if it continued for a whole year.
glossary.example: Japan's GDP fell 0.02% in the quarter, an annualised fall of 0.1%.

glossary.def: An offer of new shares to existing shareholders, usually at a discount, to raise capital.

glossary.def: Ageing tankers with obscure ownership used to ship sanctioned oil outside Western rules.

stories.everyday: Most people do not own chip shares directly, but pension funds and investment funds in Poland and elsewhere hold them, so falls like this show up in savings statements. The chips these firms make go into phones, cars and data centres, so their health matters for prices and jobs well beyond Asia.
stories.rankWhy: A 6% one-day fall in Taiwan and a 3.6% fall in South Korea hit the chipmakers that supply the whole world's AI and electronics industry, and it shows how one company's crisis can move markets across a continent.

stories.what: On Monday Taiwan's main index, the Taiex, fell 6.03% to 41,040, its second-largest points drop on record, as TSMC (the world's biggest contract chipmaker) lost about 5.7% (Investing.com). South Korea's Kospi closed 3.59% lower at about 5,100, with SK hynix down 7.89% and Samsung Electronics down about 4.5–5% (Yonhap via Korea JoongAng Daily; sources differ slightly on Samsung). Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 2.4% to about 59,662, with Kioxia down about 8% and Tokyo Electron down 7.1% (AP). Foreign investors sold a net 1.38 trillion won of Korean shares. Hong Kong's Hang Seng was the exception, ending about 0.4–0.5% higher.
stories.why: The trigger is Nvidia, the leading maker of AI chips: chief executive Jensen Huang resigned last Thursday after reports of extramarital affairs that raised US national-security concerns, and on Sunday US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the board should look outside the company for a successor (AP; CNBC). Because TSMC makes most of Nvidia's AI chips and SK hynix and Samsung supply its memory, doubts about Nvidia quickly become doubts about their future orders (Investing.com). AP said worries that AI spending growth may slow predated the scandal, and a Shinhan Securities analyst said investors were also waiting for Nvidia's results on Tuesday and Anthropic's stock-market debut this week.

stories.everyday: Oil prices feed into what Poles pay for petrol, diesel, heating and transport. Brent is still far above the roughly $72 it cost in late February before the war (AP), so any new disruption in the Gulf would show up quickly at petrol stations.
stories.rankWhy: The US–Iran war touches the Gulf, through which a large share of the world's oil travels; a third US carrier and claimed mine strikes on tankers raise the risk to energy supplies for many countries.
stories.title: A third US aircraft carrier reaches the Middle East as Iran attacks a base in Bahrain and claims tankers hit mines near Hormuz
stories.what: A US official told The National that the USS Theodore Roosevelt arrived in the area of US Central Command on Sunday, giving the US three carrier strike groups in the region. On Sunday Iran launched drones at a base in Bahrain used by US forces, its first strike on a Gulf state in weeks; Bahrain said its air defences intercepted them. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said two tankers hit naval mines and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz and that one, a supertanker, sank; Iranian state TV said five vessels hit mines in 48 hours. Reuters could not verify these claims, but the UK's maritime agency UKMTO reported an attack on a tanker in the Gulf with the crew safe (The National). On Monday the Guards' navy claimed two more tankers hit mines in the southern part of the strait, said six tankers had caught fire or were sinking since Sunday, and warned that the 'southern American-created route' is mined; none of the vessels were named and the claims were not independently confirmed (Anadolu). Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Iran is ready for either negotiations or war and will not stay in a state of 'neither war nor peace' (Anadolu).
stories.why: The war began on 28 February when the US and Israel attacked Iran over its nuclear programme, and talks to end it have stalled (The National; Anadolu). More warships signal that Washington is preparing for escalation or wants to deter it, while Iran's mine claims are a reminder that it can threaten shipping. Oil reacted only mildly: Brent dipped early in Asia and then edged up to about $96 a barrel, because the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Friday that Gulf exports are recovering and it now expects a supply surplus in the fourth quarter (Reuters; FinanceFeeds). Newsquawk said crude also eased at the open on reports, citing i24News, that the US is not considering imminent strikes on Iran.

stories.everyday: For Poland the war next door shapes defence spending, energy policy and security worries, including the risk of drones straying across borders. Russian fuel shortages and attacks on refineries can also nudge regional fuel prices.
stories.rankWhy: One of the year's largest drone attacks on Russia's capital, plus strikes on the Kerch bridge and Russian attacks on Ukraine, shows the war intensifying just as peace contacts and a Trump–Putin–Xi meeting approach.
stories.title: Ukraine sends about 600 drones towards Moscow in one of the year's largest attacks; Russia says it downed 1,336 drones overnight
stories.what: Moscow's mayor Sergei Sobyanin said about 600 drones headed towards the Moscow region between Sunday evening and Monday morning and that 191 were shot down as they approached the city (TASS; AP). Russia's Defence Ministry said its air defences destroyed 1,336 Ukrainian drones over 15 regions and the seas around Crimea, figures that cannot be independently checked. Russian officials said the Kerch Bridge to Crimea was attacked, halting road traffic until about midday, and reported people injured in the Krasnodar and Rostov regions. In Ukraine, Russian attacks killed one person in Dnipro and one in the Zaporizhzhia region, and the Ukrainian air force said it shot down 131 of 158 Russian drones.
stories.why: In a Sunday evening address, President Volodymyr Zelensky said long-range strikes had disabled more than 55% of Russia's oil-refining capacity and called them a response to Russia's refusal to de-escalate (AP via Bytes Europe). Hitting refineries and transport links aims to cut the fuel and money that sustain Russia's war effort. The attacks come after US-mediated talks in the UAE last week, the first since February, which produced plans for a large prisoner exchange (AP).

stories.everyday: When Chinese demand is weak, prices of metals like copper tend to fall, which affects companies such as Poland's KGHM. Weak Chinese consumers also mean Chinese factories push more goods abroad, which can keep prices of imported products in Europe low.
stories.rankWhy: China is the world's second-largest economy and a huge buyer and seller of goods, so a weak start to the fourth quarter affects commodity prices, exporters and growth across Asia and Europe.
stories.title: China's economy loses steam in October: retail sales grow just 0.4% and investment keeps shrinking
stories.what: China's National Bureau of Statistics said industrial output rose 4.8% in October from a year earlier, down from 5.5% in September and below the 5.3% expected in a Reuters poll. Retail sales, a measure of consumer spending in shops and online, grew only 0.4%, down from 1.1% and below forecasts of 0.8%. Fixed-asset investment (spending on things like factories, roads and buildings) fell 8.1% in January–October from a year earlier, and property investment fell 21.6%; new home prices fell further. Urban unemployment dipped to 5.1% from 5.2% (Reuters via AsiaOne).
stories.why: The figures point to weak household spending and a deepening property slump. ING's chief Greater China economist Lynn Song called the data 'a worrying start' to the fourth quarter and said more policy support would help (Reuters). An NBS spokesman said exports would keep supporting growth, while ANZ's Zhaopeng Xing expects no new stimulus this year. Macquarie economists expect Beijing to do just enough to meet its growth target, with the scale depending on how much exports slow.

stories.everyday: Ships avoiding the Red Sea must sail around Africa, which adds time and cost to goods travelling from Asia to Europe, including to Poland. The fighting also deepens one of the world's worst humanitarian crises in Yemen.
stories.rankWhy: Houthi gains near Aden and the strait of Bab al-Mandeb threaten Yemen's government and a key Red Sea shipping lane, while attacks on Saudi Arabia, including near Mecca and Medina, widen the regional war.
stories.title: Houthis reach positions about 70 km from Aden; Saudi-led coalition says it shot down drones over Mecca and Medina
stories.what: A Yemeni government military source told Xinhua that Houthi forces have moved to positions roughly 70 km from Aden, the seat of the internationally recognised government, after government forces gave up their limited gains near the Bab al-Mandeb strait about 40 days into a Saudi-backed offensive; the source called the offensive a failure. A Houthi missile attack on a checkpoint in Lahj province near Aden killed eight people and wounded 12, according to military and government sources (The New Arab). The Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed two Houthi drones over Mecca and two over Medina on Sunday, bringing the day's total to seven, after intercepting two ballistic missiles aimed at Riyadh; a Houthi spokesman called the coalition's account a fabrication (Anadolu). Houthi spokesman Yahya Sarea also claimed drones hit oil pumping stations No. 5 and No. 6 on Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline, which could not be independently verified (Xinhua). The ICRC said the Houthis released 600 captured government fighters.
stories.why: The Houthis, who are aligned with Iran, have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia since late September as part of the wider regional war, and government forces said they pulled back to defend Aden (The New Arab; Xinhua). Control of the Bab al-Mandeb, the narrow southern entrance to the Red Sea, gives the Houthis leverage over a route that carries trade between Asia and Europe.

stories.everyday: Japanese households are spending less because prices are rising faster than many incomes, a squeeze Polish readers will recognise. The yen's weakness makes Japanese cars and electronics cheaper abroad.
stories.rankWhy: Japan is the world's fourth-largest economy and its central bank is weighing a rate rise; a surprise contraction affects the yen, global bond markets and the BOJ's next step.
stories.title: Japan's economy shrinks slightly in the third quarter as consumers cut back and imports jump
stories.what: Japan's Cabinet Office said real GDP fell 0.02% in July–September from the previous quarter, an annualised fall of 0.1%, the first contraction in four quarters; economists had expected annualised growth of about 0.2–0.3% (Seoul Economic Daily; investingLive). Private consumption, about half of the economy, fell 0.3%, its second straight fall, while business investment rose 1.6%, led by AI servers and chipmaking equipment. Imports, which subtract from GDP, rose 2.5% as crude oil purchases recovered through other routes after the Strait of Hormuz closure.
stories.why: Economists said weak spending is largely due to rising prices: Meiji Yasuda's Kazutaka Maeda said it supports a Bank of Japan rate rise, while Mizuho's Ryosuke Katagi said it could strengthen resistance to further hikes on the BOJ board (Seoul Economic Daily). Markets widely expect a BOJ hike in December. A shrinking economy and rising rates pull in opposite directions, which is why the data matter for the yen, now near 160 per dollar.

stories.everyday: A stronger dollar makes dollar-priced goods such as fuel more expensive in złoty, and higher global rates can feed through to loan costs in Poland. Gold falling also affects Poles who bought gold as savings.
stories.rankWhy: Expectations of a US rate rise push up borrowing costs and the dollar worldwide, which weighs on gold, emerging-market currencies such as the złoty, and mortgage rates.
stories.title: Gold slides as markets bet on a US rate rise in December; Fed Chair Warsh speaks on Monday
stories.what: COMEX gold futures fell about 0.85% to around $3,853 an ounce on Monday after touching $3,835, and silver fell more sharply (Upstox). CME FedWatch data showed a 92% probability of a 0.25-point rise in the Fed's key rate in December and an 8% chance of a 0.5-point rise (Upstox). The Fed's target range is 3.75–4.00% after a rise in September; US consumer prices rose 0.4% in October and core prices 0.3%, more than forecast (Admiral Markets). Fed policymaker Jefferson said inflation is now the top concern and further rises are under consideration, and the Fed's Collins backed a gradual path of rises (Newsquawk). Fed Chair Kevin Warsh gives opening remarks at a San Francisco Fed conference at 18:00 Warsaw time.
stories.why: Higher expected US interest rates make interest-bearing assets such as Treasury bonds more attractive than gold, which pays no interest, and they strengthen the dollar, in which gold is priced (Upstox). The 10-year US Treasury yield ended Friday at 5.15% after producer-price data showed persistent inflation (AP). Admiral Markets noted that Warsh has said he does not favour giving advance hints about rates outside a crisis.

stories.everyday: The story shows how border rules decide whether help reaches people in time, a question that becomes life-or-death in winter.
stories.rankWhy: More than two million people in Gaza, most in makeshift shelters, face winter rain and cold while 150,000 tents wait at the border.
stories.title: Australia, Canada, Italy and the UK urge Israel to let 150,000 tents into Gaza as winter storms flood camps
stories.what: In a joint statement on 16 November, the foreign ministers of Australia, Canada, Italy and the UK said 150,000 tents and other vital supplies are being held at the border and called on Israel to open crossings and admit 'dual-use' items needed for humanitarian work (The National; Anadolu). They called the situation dire after heavy rain flooded tens of thousands of tents. The National reported that a nine-month-old baby died from cold exposure last week and that five people, including three children, were killed on 7 November when a sand bank collapsed onto tents. Ireland's Helen McEntee called at an EU foreign ministers' meeting for a stronger EU statement on aid corridors.
stories.why: 'Dual-use' items are goods with possible military as well as civilian uses, which Israel restricts on security grounds; aid groups say the restrictions slow shelter and repairs (The National). The WHO warned on Sunday that respiratory infections in Gaza are running 33,000 cases above last year's level (The New Arab).

stories.everyday: Migration policy is one of the most debated topics in EU politics, including in Poland, and how the EU shares responsibility for arrivals affects every member state.
stories.rankWhy: A record day of arrivals and a declared emergency put pressure on small island communities and on the EU's new migration rules.
stories.title: Spain declares a migration emergency in the Canary Islands after a record 1,488 people arrive in one day
stories.what: Spain's maritime rescue service rescued 1,488 people from 14 boats on Saturday, most landing on El Hierro, one of the smallest Canary Islands, beating the previous one-day record of 1,461 from November 2020 (Reuters via ThePrint; Al Jazeera). One boat carried 240 people, including 12 women and 36 children; most came from Senegal, Gambia and Guinea. Al Jazeera reported that Spain declared a migration emergency after more than 9,000 people arrived since the start of November. Arrivals from January to October were still 5.5% lower than a year earlier, government data show.
stories.why: Arrivals usually rise in autumn when the Atlantic is calmer (Reuters). The surge comes five months after the EU's Pact on Migration and Asylum took effect on 12 June 2026 (Al Jazeera). The International Organization for Migration counted at least 450 deaths on this Atlantic route in the first 10 months of the year.

stories.everyday: The risk to people in Europe is very low, but outbreaks like this show why disease control in one region matters globally, through travel, trade and aid budgets.
stories.rankWhy: Congo's deadliest Ebola outbreak has passed 11,000 cases with no approved vaccine for this strain, and it has spread to other countries.
stories.title: Congo's Ebola outbreak keeps growing: children are a quarter of cases and 400–500 new infections are recorded each week
stories.what: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has caused more than 11,000 cases and over 5,400 deaths since it was declared in mid-May, with 400 to 500 new cases a week across 67 health zones in eight provinces (allAfrica; AP). Children account for more than a quarter of confirmed infections and about a third of deaths (allAfrica). The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no known vaccine or treatment, and cases have been reported in Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria (AP).
stories.why: Armed conflict, attacks on health workers, poor roads and community mistrust have slowed tracing of people who were in contact with patients (AP; allAfrica). WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said recent attacks that killed four health workers were a major setback, leaving more than 1,000 contacts lost to follow-up (AP).

stories.everyday: Poland still relies heavily on coal, so global decisions on fossil fuels and climate finance shape the cost of its energy transition and household energy bills.
stories.rankWhy: Decisions at the UN climate talks shape energy policy and climate finance for almost every country.
stories.title: COP31 climate talks enter their final week in Antalya, split over fossil fuels and finance
stories.what: Ministers took over negotiations at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, on Monday, with a first draft of the main 'cover' decision due early in the week and the talks scheduled to end on 20 November (Hürriyet Daily News). Australia's Chris Bowen, who leads negotiations, said some of the 160 agenda items need political decisions. A proposal under discussion would raise electricity's share of global energy use to 35% by 2035; Bowen declined to say whether the draft would mention moving away from fossil fuels. The Arab Group said it would not accept targets aimed at particular energy sources.
stories.why: Climate deals need consensus, so a single bloc can block wording (Hürriyet). Developing countries also want easier access to the climate finance promised at COP29 in Baku: at least $300 billion a year by 2035.

stories.everyday: Many of these tankers pass through the Baltic near Poland's coast, so enforcement also matters for undersea cables and the risk of oil spills.
stories.rankWhy: New EU sanctions on Russia's oil-shipping network aim to cut war revenue and affect energy security and shipping across Europe.
stories.title: EU forces board a Russian 'shadow fleet' tanker; foreign ministers expected to adopt new sanctions on Monday
stories.what: EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Sunday that European naval forces boarded the tanker MV Midag in the Mediterranean and confirmed it was sailing under a false flag; tracking data list it under Zimbabwe's flag (Newsweek; Anadolu). EU foreign ministers meet in Brussels on Monday, and Commissioner Maria Luís Albuquerque said new listings targeting oil refineries and the shadow-fleet network were expected to be adopted, affecting about 100 people and entities (Agence Europe). Kallas said the EU will keep disrupting Russia's shadow fleet at sea and by diplomatic means.
stories.why: The 'shadow fleet' is a network of old tankers with unclear ownership that Russia uses to sell oil outside Western price caps and sanctions, funding its war (Agence Europe; Newsweek). Using a false flag hides who is really responsible for a ship, which also raises safety and pollution risks.

stories.everyday: Satellite internet matters for rural areas, ships, planes and militaries, including in Poland; more competition can mean lower prices for users.
stories.rankWhy: Losing 40 satellites sets back Amazon's challenge to SpaceX's Starlink and grounds one of the US's main rockets.
stories.title: ULA's Vulcan rocket fails, destroying 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites
stories.what: A United Launch Alliance (ULA) Vulcan rocket launched from Cape Canaveral at 12:40 p.m. EST on Sunday (18:40 Warsaw) suffered an anomaly about 10 minutes into flight and failed to put 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites into orbit, the company's first outright mission failure (Spaceflight Now; Anadolu). ULA said it would work with its customer to find the cause, and NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman offered help. Amazon needs more than 3,300 satellites for its network; this flight would have brought the total launched to 436 (Spaceflight Now).
stories.why: Amazon must now wait for ULA's investigation before flying on Vulcan again, and Blue Origin's New Glenn is also grounded after a May explosion, which narrows Amazon's launch options (Spaceflight Now). Satellite internet networks need thousands of satellites, so delays slow its competition with Starlink.

stories.everyday: It is a reminder that people's data is held by firms they have never heard of; anyone receiving unexpected letters or emails quoting real invoice details should treat them with caution.
stories.rankWhy: A breach touching about 22 million people, nearly one in three French residents, is one of Europe's largest recent data thefts.
stories.title: Cyberattack on La Poste subsidiary Maileva exposes data of about 22 million people in France
stories.what: On Sunday La Poste confirmed that Maileva, a digital mail subsidiary of its Docaposte unit, was hit by a cyberattack in mid-September and that about 22 million people may be affected (Next; Anadolu). Names and postal addresses of people who received documents through Maileva were taken, and Maileva says the content of documents may also have been accessed; examples reported include invoices and medical billing details. The CNIL data-protection authority was notified and the Paris prosecutor opened an investigation (Next).
stories.why: Maileva handles payslips, rent receipts, invoices and registered mail for more than 20,000 clients, including banks, insurers and public bodies, so one breach exposes data from many organisations at once (Next). Stolen personal details are often used for targeted phishing.

stories.everyday: Rules on who may buy advanced chips affect where data centres and tech jobs go, including in Central Europe.
stories.rankWhy: Ten governments are coordinating to secure chips, energy and infrastructure for AI, part of the technology rivalry with China.
stories.title: US and nine partners sign a declaration to secure supply chains for advanced AI
stories.what: The US, Australia, India, Israel, Japan, South Korea, Qatar, Singapore, the UAE and the UK signed the 'San Francisco Declaration' under the US-led Pax Silica initiative on Sunday (TRT World, citing Anadolu and the State Department). It treats economic security as part of national security and calls for diversified, trusted supply chains for technologies needed for advanced AI, with working groups on supply chains and security. The Financial Times reported that Germany, Sweden, the Netherlands and the European Commission are expected to sign next week.
stories.why: The declaration calls for reducing 'excessive dependencies' in the technologies that advanced AI relies on, including energy, transport networks and digital platforms, by building trusted alternatives (TRT World). The signing came days before a planned Trump–Xi–Putin meeting in Shenzhen.

stories.everyday: Property-company troubles in Hong Kong and mainland China show how high debt plus falling property prices can hurt savers, builders and banks.
stories.rankWhy: One of Hong Kong's biggest property developers needs a huge emergency capital raise, a sign of stress in Asian property.
stories.title: Hong Kong developer New World's shares fall as much as 47% after it plans a $3.2 billion rights issue
stories.what: New World Development's shares fell as much as 47% to a record low on Monday after it announced a HK$24.9 billion (about $3.2 billion) rights issue: shareholders are offered 11 new shares for each one they hold at HK$0.90, an 81.5% discount to the last close (Investing.com; AFP). The shares closed about 41% lower, at HK$2.885 (RTHK). Most of the money will go to repaying and servicing debt, and controlling shareholder Chow Tai Fook Enterprises will take up its full entitlement.
stories.why: A rights issue lets existing shareholders buy new shares, usually at a discount; such a large one dilutes each existing share and signals the company badly needs cash (Investing.com). The company said the plan would strengthen its finances and reduce the need to sell assets at unfavourable prices.

stories.everyday: Obesity raises the risk of diabetes and heart disease; more effective drugs could change public health, but price and access remain big questions in Poland and elsewhere.
stories.rankWhy: New weight-loss drugs are reshaping obesity treatment for hundreds of millions of people and moving some of Europe's largest companies.
stories.title: Novo Nordisk shares rise after new data show 25% average weight loss among early responders to CagriSema
stories.what: In analyses of its REDEFINE 1 trial presented at ObesityWeek 2026, Novo Nordisk said people who lost at least 5% of their weight within eight weeks of starting CagriSema went on to lose an average 25.4% by week 68 (Investing.com; Reuters). Digestive side effects affected 79.6% of patients on the drug versus 39.9% on placebo. Novo called the findings exploratory analyses done after the trial; it expects a US regulatory decision in the fourth quarter. Its shares rose about 2.4% (Reuters; Investing.com).
stories.why: CagriSema combines semaglutide, the ingredient in Wegovy, with cagrilintide; showing which patients respond strongly could help doctors and insurers target it (Investing.com). The drug is not yet approved in the United States.

stories.everyday: The Tribunal checks whether laws respect the constitution; a dispute over who legitimately sits on it creates legal uncertainty for courts, businesses and citizens.
stories.rankWhy: The fight over Poland's Constitutional Tribunal decides who can rule on whether laws are constitutional, affecting the rule of law and EU relations.
stories.title: Poland: presidential talks on the Constitutional Tribunal take place on Monday without KO and the Left
stories.what: The head of the President's Chancellery, Zbigniew Bogucki, leads talks on the Constitutional Tribunal at the Belweder palace at 14:00 on Monday; President Karol Nawrocki will not attend (RMF24). PSL, Polska 2050, Razem, Konfederacja, PiS and Rozwój Plus confirmed attendance, while Koalicja Obywatelska and the Left said they would not come. PSL and Polska 2050 are bringing a draft 'constitutional reset' law; KO's Cezary Tomczyk said the idea is unrealistic because the Sejm lacks the two-thirds majority needed (Rzeczpospolita).
stories.why: On 30 October judges elected in this Sejm term said the most senior judge, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, had taken over the Tribunal and suspended its president Bogdan Święczkowski; he called it a usurpation and Nawrocki said the constitutional order had been violated, while Prime Minister Donald Tusk says the president refused to swear in some new judges (RMF24).

stories.everyday: Cape Verde's large diaspora, which sends money home, is one reason turnout is low, a pattern also seen in countries with many emigrants, including Poland in the past.
stories.rankWhy: A peaceful re-election in one of Africa's most stable democracies, though with low turnout.
stories.title: Cape Verde's President José Maria Neves wins a second term; challenger Joana Rosa concedes
stories.what: Provisional results from 97% of polling stations gave Neves 63.8% of the vote, enough to avoid a run-off, against 31.6% for Joana Rosa, a former justice minister and the country's first woman presidential candidate (Reuters via CNBC Africa; allAfrica). Fewer than one-third of eligible voters took part. Rosa conceded and congratulated Neves.
stories.why: Neves, from the centre-left PAICV, has been president since 2021 after 15 years as prime minister; Rosa's centre-right MpD lost power in a May legislative vote (Reuters). Neves linked the low turnout partly to citizens living abroad and proposed electronic voting.

stories.everyday: Poland is not a member, but such bodies show how language and history still shape international alliances.
stories.rankWhy: Members of the French-speaking world's main organisation could not agree on a leader.
stories.title: Francophonie summit postpones the election of its secretary-general by a year
stories.what: Leaders at the 20th Francophonie summit in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, put off choosing a secretary-general for 2027–2030 after hours of tense talks; Louise Mushikiwabo of Rwanda will stay in office until November 2027 to lead institutional reforms but cannot run again (Anadolu, French service). Several states wanted Romania's Dacian Cioloș chosen by consensus, while Rwanda pushed for a vote, according to Anadolu's sources.
stories.why: The organisation's rules, revised in 2022, favour consensus but allow a secret ballot by simple majority; Congo also had a candidate, Juliana Lumumba, in a race where Rwanda backed the incumbent (Anadolu).

stories.everyday: Much of the world's trade, including goods shipped to Europe, passes through the South China Sea.
stories.rankWhy: China and Southeast Asia trade more than $1 trillion a year, but disputes in the South China Sea remain unresolved.
stories.title: China's Premier Li Qiang praises ties with ASEAN in Manila, but the South China Sea code of conduct is still unfinished
stories.what: Chinese Premier Li Qiang arrived in Manila for the 29th China–ASEAN summit and pledged to defend multilateralism and free trade, citing trade of over $1 trillion a year (Anadolu; China-Global South Project). The ASEAN summit did not complete a long-negotiated code of conduct for the South China Sea, and Indonesia's president urged both sides to conclude it. At the ASEAN–UN summit, UN Secretary-General António Guterres called for a 'safe, voluntary' return of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar (Anadolu).
stories.why: Several ASEAN members, including the Philippines, have overlapping claims with China in the South China Sea, a busy shipping route; a code of conduct would set rules to avoid clashes (general background).

stories.everyday: Any thaw between two nuclear-armed neighbours lowers the risk of a conflict that could disrupt trade and travel far beyond South Asia.
stories.rankWhy: A small step in contacts between two nuclear-armed rivals that fought a four-day conflict in May 2025.
stories.title: Pakistan's climate minister will visit India for an SCO meeting, the first federal ministerial trip since 2023
stories.what: Pakistan's foreign ministry said Climate Change Minister Musadik Malik will attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation's Civilizational Dialogue in New Delhi on 20–22 November (Manila Times). It would be the first visit to India by a Pakistani federal minister since Bilawal Bhutto Zardari went to an SCO meeting in Goa in May 2023.
stories.why: Relations have been frozen since the May 2025 conflict, which followed an attack that killed over two dozen tourists in Kashmir; India accuses Pakistan of backing the attack, which Pakistan denies (Manila Times).

stories.everyday: Fans travelling abroad are subject to local law; fines and bans can follow even when no charges are brought.
stories.rankWhy: More than a hundred people, mostly Polish fans, were detained abroad after football violence.
stories.title: 105 people, mostly Poles, detained in Bucharest after clashes around the Romania–Poland match
stories.what: After clashes following Saturday's Nations League match between Romania and Poland, 105 people, mostly Polish citizens, were detained in Bucharest (TVN24). Polish Foreign Ministry spokesman Maciej Wewiór said all were released, but 89 Polish citizens were fined.
stories.why: Police and football authorities treat away-fan violence as a public-order risk; detentions abroad involve consular help from the home country (TVN24).

stories.everyday: Rail sabotage can delay trains and raises the cost of protecting critical infrastructure.
stories.rankWhy: Official findings on sabotage of a key rail line to Ukraine matter for Poland's security.
stories.title: Polish rail investigators classify incidents on the Warsaw–Dorohusk line as terrorism-related
stories.what: Poland's rail accident investigation commission published reports on two incidents from November 2025 on line 7 from Warsaw to Dorohusk, near the Ukrainian border: an explosive detonated under a freight wagon near Mika, and overhead wire was stolen near Gołąb (TVN24). The commission classified one as a terrorist act and the other as a potential terrorist threat.
stories.why: The line leads to the Ukrainian border crossing at Dorohusk, so disruptions there affect a key transport route to Ukraine.

stories.everyday: Like Poland's matura, Enem results decide university places, so participation affects young people's chances.
stories.rankWhy: University entrance in Latin America's largest country depends on this exam, and record absence worries educators.
stories.title: Brazil: 32% of candidates skip the first day of the Enem university entrance exam, the highest since the pandemic
stories.what: On the first day of Brazil's national secondary-school exam, Enem, 32% of registered candidates were absent, up from 27% in 2025 (The Rio Times). The education minister blamed automatic enrolment of public-school pupils.
stories.why: Automatic registration adds students who may not intend to sit the exam, which inflates absence rates (The Rio Times).

stories.everyday: Deposit protection and honest supervision are what make it safe to keep savings in a bank, in Paraguay or Poland.
stories.rankWhy: A failed digital bank and a criminal probe reaching the central bank test trust in Paraguay's financial system.
stories.title: Paraguay central bank's legal director surrenders to police in the Ueno Bank collapse case
stories.what: Aldo Rodríguez, legal director of Paraguay's central bank, surrendered at a police station in Asunción on Sunday; prosecutors suspect him in the case of Ueno, a digital bank that failed and was shut by the central bank in early November (The Rio Times). Prosecutors allege a report to the Senate left out warnings about the bank's insolvency.
stories.why: Insolvency means a bank's debts exceed its assets; if supervisors knew and hid it, depositors could not protect themselves (The Rio Times).

stories.everyday: Shifts in global investment show how money moves between countries, affecting their currencies and borrowing costs, including emerging markets like Poland.
stories.rankWhy: Record foreign buying of Indian shares shows money moving out of tech-heavy Asian markets.
stories.title: Foreign investors pour a record $8.9 billion into Indian shares in November
stories.what: Foreign investors bought a net $8.9 billion of Indian equities so far in November, the largest monthly inflow since records began in 2002 (HDFC Sky). India's Sensex rose in Monday morning trade while Taiwan and Korea fell sharply (Business Standard; AP).
stories.why: Analysts cited by HDFC Sky said investors may rotate from tech-heavy Asian markets towards India's domestic sectors, and lower oil prices help India, a big oil importer.

stories.everyday: Poland is also attracting data-centre investment, so the same debate over power and water use may arrive here.
stories.rankWhy: Local opposition to energy- and water-hungry AI data centres is growing in Europe.
stories.title: Thousands protest in Edinburgh against plans for large AI data centres in Scotland
stories.what: Thousands of people marched in Edinburgh against plans for large-scale AI data centres in Scotland (Anadolu).
stories.why: Data centres use large amounts of electricity and often water for cooling, which raises concerns about energy prices, the environment and land use.

stories.everyday: Such bans show the trade-off between security and freedom of communication that many countries face.
stories.rankWhy: Blocking a widely used messaging app affects millions of users' communication.
stories.title: Jordan blocks Telegram, citing the fight against extremism
stories.what: Jordan blocked the messaging app Telegram, saying the step is meant to counter extremism and radicalisation (Anadolu).
stories.why: Jordan's authorities link the app to extremist content; blocking a whole platform also cuts off ordinary users, which is why such bans are debated as a free-expression issue.

stories.everyday: Moldova borders Ukraine and Romania; its stability matters for the EU's eastern flank, including Poland.
stories.rankWhy: Votes in Moldova's pro-Russian autonomous region matter for an EU candidate country on Ukraine's border.
stories.title: Moldova: elections in the autonomous region of Gagauzia declared valid as turnout passes 25%
stories.what: Elections for the bashkan (governor) and the People's Assembly of Gagauzia, an autonomous region of Moldova, are valid because turnout exceeded the legal 25% threshold, according to preliminary data from the Central Election Commission (Anadolu).
stories.why: A minimum-turnout rule means a vote only counts if enough of the electorate takes part; here the 25% bar was cleared (Anadolu).

stories.everyday: Extreme weather strains emergency services and farms, which can affect food prices.
stories.rankWhy: Floods and wildfires are hitting different parts of Bolivia at the same time.
stories.title: Bolivia's army joins flood response in Cochabamba as a wildfire passes 8,000 hectares
stories.what: Bolivia's army joined the flood response in Cochabamba while a wildfire burned more than 8,000 hectares (The Rio Times).
stories.why: Heavy rain in one region and dry conditions in another can happen at once in a large country with varied climates.

stories.everyday: Mountain rescuers urge hikers to check avalanche warnings and carry safety equipment in winter.
stories.rankWhy: A personal tragedy and a warning about early-season avalanche danger in the Tatras.
stories.title: Tourist killed by an avalanche in Poland's Tatra mountains
stories.what: On Sunday before noon a tourist near Żółta Turnia was swept by an avalanche towards Dolina Pańszczyca and buried; rescuers could not save him (TVN24).
stories.why: Fresh snow on steep slopes early in the season can be unstable.

stories.everyday: Drug trafficking still drives violence and migration in the Americas.
stories.rankWhy: The death of a notorious cartel founder closes a chapter in Mexico's drug-war history.
stories.title: Guadalajara Cartel founder Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo dies aged 80
stories.what: Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, founder of the Guadalajara Cartel, died on Sunday in a Guadalajara hospital, aged 80; reports cite multiple organ failure (The Rio Times). He was convicted over the 1985 killing of US DEA agent Enrique Camarena and spent about 37 years in prison.
stories.why: His organisation is often described as a forerunner of Mexico's later drug cartels.

stories.everyday: Afrobeat and its successor Afrobeats are now heard worldwide, including in Poland.
stories.rankWhy: A cultural milestone for African music.
stories.title: Fela Kuti becomes the first African artist inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame; Glenn Close wins her first Oscar
stories.what: Nigerian Afrobeat pioneer Fela Kuti was inducted posthumously in the Early Influence category at a ceremony in Los Angeles, the first African artist so honoured (allAfrica); Wu-Tang Clan, Phil Collins and Queen Latifah were also inducted (Anadolu). At the Governors Awards, actress Glenn Close received an Oscar after eight nominations (Anadolu).
stories.why: Such honours reflect how African music has influenced global pop, hip-hop and jazz.

stories.everyday: It shows how long-lasting basic science missions can be: Voyager has worked for almost 50 years.
stories.rankWhy: A symbolic scientific milestone for humanity's most distant spacecraft.
stories.title: Voyager 1 will become the first human-made object one light-day from Earth on Wednesday
stories.what: On Wednesday 18 November at 10:16 GMT (11:16 Warsaw), Voyager 1, launched on 5 September 1977, will be about 25.9 billion km from Earth, the distance light travels in a day; a signal will take at least 48 hours to go there and back (Anadolu).
stories.why: Light travels about 300,000 km per second, so in 24 hours it covers roughly 25.9 billion km.
